text: Last lesson showed that sample means form their own distribution with spread equal to sigma over the square root of n. That spread has a name: the standard error. It answers the most practical question in estimation — if I repeated this study, how far would my estimate typically move? A small standard error means your sample mean is a reliable guide to the population mean; a large one means treat it with suspicion.

These two are constantly confused. Standard deviation describes how spread out individual observations are. Standard error describes how spread out a statistic, like the sample mean, would be across repeated samples. Standard deviation is a property of your data; standard error is a property of your estimate. The formula is s divided by the square root of n, where s is the sample standard deviation.

Simulating a population of 200,000 orders with true mean 39.71 and standard deviation 26.16, then drawing one sample of 50: the sample mean is 37.45, with a sample standard deviation of 26.67 and a standard error of 3.77. Read that as — samples of 50 from this population typically produce means within a few units of the truth, and ours is 2.3 below the true value, comfortably within one standard error.

Notice ddof equals 1 — it divides by n minus 1 instead of n, giving an unbiased estimate of spread, 26.67 versus 26.40 with ddof equals 0. pandas's dot std already uses ddof equals 1, but numpy's np.std does not — a common trap. scipy's stats.sem computes the standard error for you directly.

Drawing samples of 25, 100, 400, and 1600: the standard error drops from 3.93 to 3.41 to 1.29 to 0.6. Quadrupling the sample roughly halves the standard error. Precision costs a lot — to go from a standard error of about 3.8 down to 1.0 with this data, you'd need roughly 711 observations.

Does s over root n really match the spread of means across repeated samples? Drawing 5,000 samples of 50 and finding the standard deviation of their means gives 3.71 — matching the theoretical prediction of 3.70 almost exactly. The standard error really is just the standard deviation of the sampling distribution.

The idea generalizes to any statistic. For a proportion, like 120 of 400 customers returning an order, the standard error is the square root of p times 1 minus p, over n — here about 2.3 percentage points. For a difference between two independent group means, the variances add — a difference of 2.0 with a standard error of 0.70 is nearly three standard errors from zero, an idea that leads straight into hypothesis testing.

The standard error only measures random sampling error — it says nothing about bias. A badly collected sample can have a tiny standard error and still be far from the truth. It also assumes independent observations, and its normal interpretation relies on the CLT. To recap: standard deviation describes individual data, standard error describes the precision of an estimate, it shrinks slowly with more data, and it applies to proportions and differences too — but it always ignores bias.
